title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure carried by synthetic media. An AI-generated video presented a well-known financial sector personality as endorsing an investment with claimed significant returns, and the victim acted on that apparent endorsement. The falsehood sat in the likeness itself rather than in a written claim or a compromised account, which is what makes this class of fraud hard to spot from the advertisement alone.

The failure occurred at the very front of the transaction, in the promotional video, before any regulated provider or account was involved. Everything after it, the move to WhatsApp, the help opening multiple accounts, the remote access to the victim's computer, the pressure to borrow, depended on the victim still believing the endorsement was real. Catching it would have required independently verifying that the person shown had actually made the endorsement, and confirming that the financial services provider was authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, which is the check the police pointed to.

What is not established is who the personality was, since the PSNI did not name them, and the reporting does not show that any real person consented to or took part in the video. The police account describes a fraud under investigation, not a finding against any individual.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 to an artificial intelligence scam, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said. The victim saw an AI generated video that appeared to feature a well known financial sector personality. It advertised an investment with claimed significant returns. After a small initial investment, the scammers contacted the victim on WhatsApp and pushed for more payments. They helped create multiple accounts and gained remote access to the victim's computer, then persuaded the victim to borrow money. The funds went to accounts controlled by criminals.

The PSNI called it a sophisticated and substantial fraud. It did not name the celebrity, though BBC News NI has seen similar scams using financial experts Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett. Police said apparent celebrity endorsements do not prove an investment is real. Superintendent Joanne Gibson of the Scamwise Partnership urged people to pause and check financial activity and to talk to relatives about fraud. Police advised independently verifying who people are dealing with, checking that financial services providers are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.
